## Loading Data and Libraries

```{r}
library("tidyverse")
library("broom")
library("cowplot")

biopsy <- read_csv("https://wilkelab.org/classes/SDS348/data_sets/biopsy.csv")
```

## Data description

## PCA

Principal Component Analysis is a computational method that aims to project high dimensional data points (multiple variables) into a lower dimensional space explained by the principal components, which is usually 2 dimensions for ease of visualization. The principal components are chosen to explain where the highest variance is in the data.

```{r}
pca_fit <- biopsy |>  
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>  # retain only numeric columns
  prcomp(scale = TRUE) # do PCA on scaled data
```

```{r}
pca_fit |> 
  augment(biopsy) |>  # add original dataset back in
  ggplot(aes(.fittedPC1, .fittedPC2, color = outcome)) + 
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(malignant = "tomato", benign = "navy")
  ) +
  theme_cowplot() + background_grid()
```

This plot shows a clear difference between malignant and benign given the first two principle components.

```{r}
pca_fit |> 
  tidy(matrix = "rotation")
```

This shows the rotation matrix which holds the coordinates fro the PCs (these are vectors) in the data space. These vectors are then used as the axis in the PCA.

```{r}
pca_fit |> 
  tidy(matrix = "eigenvalues") |> 
  ggplot(aes(PC, percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "limegreen", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))
  ) +
  theme_grey(12)
```

This plot shows how much each PC explains the data. Here we can see that PC1 explains roughly 65 % of the data while the rest of the PCs all explain less than 10. In the first plot it was clear that PC1 showed a pretty clear difference between malignant and benign.
